As described in section 21.5.1, the initial period for which penalties may be determined, both for failing to disclose the scheme and for failing to comply with an order made under section 308A relating to the scheme, starts the day after the end of the prescribed period, and the initial period ends with the earlier of:

the day on which the tribunal determines penalties

the last day before the day on which the scheme is disclosed or the promoter complies with the relevant section 308A order

The amount of the initial daily penalty is determined by the First-tier Tribunal (section 21.5.2 and section 21.5.3 has more information).

If the promoter had reasonable grounds to believe that the scheme was not disclosable before the issue of the order, the order removes that doubt.

The law provides that the promoter cannot rely on doubt as to notifiability as a reasonable excuse for not providing the prescribed information about the scheme within 10 days of the tribunal making the order.

This does not mean that penalties will definitely be determined against on the promoter if it does not provide the prescribed information within 10 days of the order.

However, any contention the promoter makes that it should not be made liable for penalties because it has a reasonable excuse cannot depend on there being doubt about whether or not the scheme is notifiable.

If the promoter does not disclose the scheme within 10 business days of the order being made, the maximum amount of both the initial daily penalty (which may be determined by a tribunal) and the secondary daily penalty (which may be determined by HMRC) increase to £5,000 for each day that the failure continues after the 10 days.

Weekends, bank holidays, Good Friday and Christmas Day are not counted in calculating the 10 business days.

This higher daily penalty is in addition to any penalties at up to £600 for the period ending 11 days after the date on which the order was issued.

Where a tribunal has made an order under section 310A requiring more information about a scheme in respect of which a tribunal has given an order under section 314A, the maximum penalty for failing to comply with the section 310A order is £5,000 a day.

If the maximum penalty the tribunal can set using the daily penalty described is less than £1 million for the initial period, it may set a higher penalty of up to £1 million in some circumstances. When making this decision the tribunal will take into account all considerations it considers relevant, including particularly the aim of deterring that person or other persons from failing to comply in a similar way.

21.5.5 Cases where a section 306A order has been issued

A section 306A order issued by a tribunal determines that a scheme is to be treated as notifiable. It must be disclosed within 10 business days, beginning with the day after the order is made (section 20.6).

After a section 306A order, the initial period for which penalties may be determined both for failing to disclose the scheme and for failing to comply with a section 308A notice relating to the scheme starts on the 11th business day after the order is made.

This initial period ends with the earlier of:

the day on which the tribunal determines penalties

the last day before the day, on which the scheme is disclosed or the promoter complies with the section 308A notice

The amount of the initial daily penalty is determined by the First-tier Tribunal (section 21.5.2 and section 21.5.3).

The law provides that the promoter cannot rely on doubt as to notifiability as a reasonable excuse preventing the imposition of penalties if it does not provide the prescribed information within 10 business days of the section 306A order.

If the promoter does not disclose the scheme within 10 business days of the order, the maximum amount of the initial daily penalty (which may be determined by a tribunal) and the secondary daily penalty (which may be determined by HMRC) is the higher amount of £5,000 rather than £600. Weekends, bank holidays, Good Friday and Christmas Day are not counted in calculating the 10 days.

If a tribunal subsequently issues an order under section 314A or the person agrees that the scheme was disclosable and that they were required to have disclosed it before the section 306A order was made, HMRC may apply to the tribunal to determine a further penalty. This penalty will relate to the period starting on the date by which the scheme should have been disclosed and ending 10 business days after the section 306A order or, if earlier, on the day before the prescribed information was provided.

Any backdated penalty would be at the lower maximum rate of £600 per day.

Where a tribunal has made an order under section 310A requiring more information about a scheme in respect of which a tribunal has given an order under section 306A, the maximum penalty for failing to comply with the section 310A order is £5,000 a day.

If the maximum penalty the tribunal can set using the daily penalty described is less than £1 million for the initial period, it may set a higher penalty of up to £1 million in some circumstances.

When making this decision the tribunal will take into account all considerations it considers relevant, including particularly the aim of deterring that person or other persons from failing to comply in a similar way.

21.6 Other Information penalties

Information penalties apply to the following instances of failure to provide prescribed information by the due date and in the form and manner specified in this guidance:

a promoter who does not respond to a pre-disclosure enquiry when required to do so (section 20.4.1 and section 20.4.2 have more information)

an introducer who does not provide, when required to do so, the identity of the person who supplied them with information about the scheme or persons with whom the introducer has made marketing contacts (section 20.4.3 has more information)

a promoter or person involved with the supply of a scheme who does not provide their client with a scheme reference number and with the further required information as supplied for this purpose by HMRC (section 16.2 has more information)

a client of a promoter or of a supplier who fails to provide the scheme reference number to any other person whom they might reasonably expect to be a party to the scheme and expected to obtain a tax advantage from using it (section 16.3 includes employers failing to provide the scheme reference number to an employee for a scheme implemented by the employer in relation to that employee’s employment — it does not matter for this purpose whether the tax advantage is expected to be obtained by the employer only, the employee only or both)

a promoter or other supplier who fails to provide HMRC with details of a client to whom they are obliged to issue a scheme reference number (section 19 has more information)

a promoter or other supplier that does not supply further information on parties to the arrangement when required to do so by written notice (section 20 has more information)

an employer who fails to provide the scheme reference number to employees in relation to whose employments a tax advantage is expected to arise (section 14.3.1 has more information)

an employer who fails to provide HMRC with information about employees to whom it is required to provide a scheme reference number (section 16.8 has more information)

a client who does not provide to a promoter or supplier their National Insurance number, UTR or assurances that neither applies (section 16.4 has more information)

a person who fails to tell HMRC the scheme reference number notified to them by a promoter or supplier and the time when the person expects to obtain the tax advantage under the arrangements (section 14.5 has more information)

a promoter or supplier who fails to provide updated information about themselves and the scheme (section 14.9.1 has more information)

In each case the failure includes cases where information is provided after the end of the period prescribed in the Information Regulations (SI 2012/1836) or in a format other than that specified in the DOTAS guidance.

For all of the information penalties listed, a tribunal may determine an initial penalty for each failure of an amount not exceeding £5,000.

HMRC may determine a daily penalty, not exceeding £600, for each day that each failure to provide information continues after an initial penalty has been determined.

The maximum daily penalty for all failures increases from £600 a day to £5000 per day starting on the 11th business day after an order has been made under section 306A or 314A.

21.7 The user penalty — tax advantage

A scheme user who fails to comply with a section 313 obligation to report a scheme reference number and related information (on a return or separately, as prescribed in the Information Regulations (SI 2012/1836)) is from 26 March 2015 liable to a penalty of:

£5,000 per scheme (for example, each scheme to which the failure relates) for a first occasion

£7,500 per scheme on the second occasion within 3 years (whether or not it relates to the same scheme involved in the previous occasion)

£10,000 per scheme on the third and subsequent occasions (whether or not the failure relates to schemes involved in a previous occasion)

Before that date the penalty was £100 for a first occasion, £500 for a second occasion and £1,000 on third and subsequent occasions.

A scheme user, who is required to report this information on a return does not satisfy their obligations under section 313 unless they enter the information in the boxes provided for that purpose on the return.

For instance, including the scheme reference number or numbers in the ‘white space’ box on returns does not meet the user’s obligation to report the scheme reference number.

You may incur penalties up to £10,000 per scheme if you do not report the scheme reference number on your return in the boxes on the return specified for this purpose or in the form and manner specified if a report is to be made separately from a return. These penalties are determined by HMRC.

21.8 Failures involving both disclosable National Insurance contribution arrangements and disclosable Income Tax arrangements (SI 2012/1868, reg 22(14))

No penalty will be charged for a failure to disclose a National Insurance contribution arrangement if the arrangement, or substantially the same arrangement, is also a disclosable Income Tax arrangement and a penalty has been determined for failing to disclose that arrangement.

The same principle applies in relation to information and user penalties.

21.9 The user penalty — National Insurance contributions advantage

A scheme user who fails to report a scheme reference number and related information on form AAG4, in relation to a scheme which is expected to obtain only an National Insurance contributions advantage (and no tax advantage), is from 21 December 2017 liable to a penalty of:

£5,000 per scheme (for example, each scheme to which the failure relates) for a first occasion

£7,500 per scheme on the second occasion within 3 years (whether or not it relates to the same scheme involved in the previous occasion)

£10,000 per scheme on the third and subsequent occasions (whether or not the failure relates to schemes involved in a previous occasion)

Before that date the penalty was £100 for a first occasion, £500 for a second occasion and £1,000 on third and subsequent occasions.

You may incur penalties up to £10,000 per scheme if you do not report the scheme reference number using form AAG4. These penalties are determined by HMRC.

21A. Penalties: Penalties under sections 315 and 315A FA 2004, determined by HMRC on or after 18 March 2026

21A.1 General

From 18 March 2026 the power to impose penalties on any person who has failed to comply with their DOTAS obligations moved from the Tribunal to HMRC. For guidance in relation to penalty proceedings which HMRC started before 18 March 2026. (Read section 21).

HMRC’s focus is on enabling scheme promoters and users to comply with their DOTAS obligations. However, a penalty regime is necessary to deter non-compliant behaviours.

A person who fails to comply with a DOTAS reporting obligation is liable to a penalty under section 315 FA 2004. A penalty imposed under this section is treated as a penalty under the Taxes Management Act 1970 and is therefore determined and imposed by an authorised officer of HMRC under section 100(1) Taxes Management Act 1970.

DOTAS penalties fall into 3 categories.

Disclosure penalties apply to failure to disclose a scheme. There are variations in cases where a tribunal has issued a disclosure order.

Information penalties.

User penalties — apply to failure by a scheme user to report a scheme reference number to HMRC.

Disclosure penalties and Information penalties involve an initial penalty and a further daily penalty if non-compliance continues. Some of the initial penalties, including the penalty for failing to disclose a notifiable scheme, are also calculated as a daily penalty.

HMRC must make the penalty determination within 6 years after the date on which the penalty was incurred (section 103 TMA 1970).

21A.2 Appeals and Reviews

Section 315B of FA 2004 applies the provisions of Part 10 TMA 1970 in relation to the assessment of DOTAS penalties. Where an authorised officer has determined the amount of a penalty, the amount charged is payable within 30 days of the date of issue of the notice of determination. This is under section 100A of TMA 1970.

There is a right of appeal against the penalty determination under section 100B TMA 1970. Accordingly, if a person who receives a notice of penalty determination disagrees with HMRC’s decision to charge a penalty they can appeal by writing to HMRC and say why they think the decision is wrong. They need to do this within 30 days of the notice telling them about the penalty determination. HMRC will then contact them to try and settle the matter.

If an agreement cannot be reached, HMRC will write to the relevant person to explain the reasons why and set out their view of the matter.

That person can then (either):

have the matter reviewed by an impartial officer who works for HMRC Legal Group and who specialises in review work

take their appeal to an independent tribunal

Most disagreements can be resolved by HMRC Legal Group reviewing the matter, without the need to take the appeal to a tribunal. Often a review is quicker and costs less than taking an appeal to a tribunal.

If the person disagrees with the outcome of the review by HMRC Legal Group, an appeal can be made to the tribunal. This must be done within 30 days of the date of the letter setting out the outcome of the review.

If an appeal is made, HMRC will not ask for the penalty to be paid whilst the appeal is being considered.

If you disagree with a tax decision or penalty, follow the guidance for more information about appeal and review rights. Full guidance is also available in the appeals and reviews tribunals manual.

21A.3 Reasonable excuse

A person will not be liable to a penalty for failing to do something within a limited period of time if an officer of HMRC gives the person more time to provide information to HMRC and the person then provides that information before the end of that extended time limit (section 315C Finance Act 2004).

A person will also not be liable to a penalty for a failure if they both:

have a reasonable excuse

put the failure right without unreasonable delay after the excuse has ended

It is for the person who failed to comply with a DOTAS obligation to show that they had a reasonable excuse at the time of the failure.

There is no statutory definition of ‘reasonable excuse’ or ‘unreasonable delay’. Both phrases must be given their ordinary meaning.

The Upper Tribunal’s comments in the case of Christine Perrin [2018] UKUT 0156 (TCC), provide guidance on how the authorised officer and a tribunal would be expected to approach reasonable excuse — read paragraphs 69 to 71 and 81.

HMRC considers reasonable excuse to be something that stops a person from meeting an obligation, despite them having taken reasonable care to meet that obligation.

To be a reasonable excuse for failing to meet an obligation, the excuse must exist on or before the date of the obligation. If the excuse does not arise until after that date and the obligation has not been met, it cannot be a reasonable excuse for that failure.

Whether the person has a reasonable excuse will depend on the circumstances in which the failure occurred and the individual experience, knowledge and other attributes of the person who has failed. Each case must be considered individually on the facts and in view of the person’s abilities and circumstances.

A combination of events, that on their own may not be a reasonable excuse, may be a reasonable excuse when considered together. If there is a reasonable excuse it must exist throughout the period of default.

If the circumstances that cause the person to have a reasonable excuse end, the excuse is treated as continuing if the person puts right the act or omission and does so without unreasonable delay after the excuse ends.

If a person is found to have had a reasonable excuse for a failure and corrected that failure without unreasonable delay, then they will not have to pay a penalty.

But if the person does not put right the failure without unreasonable delay after the excuse has ended, they will not have a reasonable excuse and will remain liable to a penalty.

The compliance handbook gives further guidance about reasonable excuse.

21A.3.1 Reasonable excuse — reason to consider a scheme is not disclosable

HMRC will consider a person to have a reasonable excuse for not disclosing a scheme where they are satisfied that there were reasonable grounds to consider that the scheme was not disclosable. What is reasonable in such circumstances depends upon the particular facts.

HMRC does not consider that the fact alone that a person has not disclosed a scheme on the basis of legal advice would provide a reasonable excuse. HMRC considers that the proper test here, in the DOTAS context, is whether it was reasonable for a particular person to rely upon the particular advice received in relation to the particular facts of the case.

The factors HMRC will consider in relation to a promoter may include the following:

the level of knowledge the promoter had, or might reasonably be expected to have, of DOTAS

the level of knowledge the promoter had, or might reasonably be expected to have, of the tax system generally and of the specific parts engaged by the scheme

whether the promoter provided the legal adviser with full and accurate information about the scheme and any other factors that might affect how DOTAS applies, including in relation to the DOTAS hallmarks

whether any of the details of the scheme in dispute differ significantly from those of the scheme to which the legal advice relates

whether any analysis or assumption made by the instructing promoter was correct and reasonable, for example whether assumptions about the level of trading income participants may receive are reasonable and supported by evidence in a tax loss scheme

to what degree does the legal advice take account of previous DOTAS decisions by the tribunal and explain why the scheme is not disclosable, by reference to the relevant tests in the DOTAS legislation

In cases where a disclosure order is issued by the tribunal (section 20.5) any reasonable excuse which relies on doubt as to whether the arrangements are notifiable ends 10 days following the day that the tribunal issues the order. This includes instances where the promoter has legal advice that the arrangements are not notifiable.

The compliance handbook gives further guidance about reasonable excuse.

21A.3.2.1 Limitations to defence of reasonable excuse — monitored promoters and their clients

A monitored promoter is a promoter to which a First-tier Tribunal has approved the issue of a monitoring notice under sections 242 to 244 of the Finance Act 2014. Read section 3.1.

The objectives of the monitored promoter rules are to change the behaviour of a small and persistent minority of promoters of avoidance schemes who are not transparent with HMRC and display other behaviours detrimental to the fairness of the tax system.

A monitored promoter cannot rely on legal advice as a reasonable excuse in connection with the charging of penalties in respect of failing to meet any of its duties under the DOTAS rules if:

the advice was not based on a full and accurate description of the facts

the conclusions in the advice were unreasonable

Where a client of a non-resident monitored promoter fails to notify HMRC in accordance with s309 of the Finance Act 2004, any legal advice given or procured by the monitored promoter is to be ignored in determining whether the person has a reasonable excuse for that failure in connection with the charging of penalties in respect of that failure.

Similarly, where a person has entered into a transaction that is part of arrangements for which there is no promoter under DOTAS and that person fails to provide information to HMRC in accordance with s310 of the Finance Act 2004, any legal advice given or procured by a monitored promoter is to be ignored in determining whether the person has a reasonable excuse for that failure in connection with the charging of penalties in respect of that failure.

21A.4 Penalties for failing to comply with sections 308(1) and (3), 309, 310, 310A and 311C Finance Act 2004

21A.4.1 Cases where no disclosure order is made

The guidance in section 21A.4 relates to cases where no disclosure order is made by the Tribunal (read section 21A.7 for cases where a disclosure order is made).

21A.4.2 Penalties for failing to comply with sections 308, 309 and 310 when HMRC has allocated an SRN after a promoter or user has disclosed the scheme

A person who discloses a notifiable scheme before HMRC allocates an SRN is liable to a penalty if the disclosure is either not made until after the due date or is not made in the specified form and manner. With one exception, the person is liable to a penalty of up to a maximum of £600 per day in a set period.

The set period starts on the day after the due date by which the person was required to disclose the scheme (read section 21A.4.5). The first day of the period is the day on which the failure to comply began.

The set period ends on the day before whichever of these is earliest:

the person complies with the duty

the authorised officer determines the penalty

The maximum penalty may be increased up to £1 million if the authorised officer considers that the amount of penalty would be inappropriately low if it was limited to £600 a day. An authorised officer must take account of all relevant considerations when making the decision that the penalty would be inappropriately low if it were not increased to up to £1 million. (Read section 21A.6)..

21A.4.3 Penalties for failing to comply with section 308 when no disclosure has been made to HMRC before HMRC allocates an SRN

A promoter who fails to disclose a notifiable scheme is liable for a penalty. Although not legally required to have done so, in such cases HMRC will commonly have given a notice under section 310D Finance Act 2004 (read section 13.4). to a person it reasonably suspects of being a promoter.

With one exception, the person is liable to a penalty of up to a maximum of £600 per day in a set period.

The set period starts on the day after the due date by which the person was required to disclose the scheme (read section 21A.4.5). The first day of the period is the day on which the failure to comply began.

The set period ends on the earliest of the day before:

the day on which the person complies with the duty later than the due date

the day on which a scheme reference number is allocated to the arrangements or proposed arrangements

the day on which the authorised officer determines the penalty

The maximum penalty may be increased up to £1 million if the authorised officer considers that the amount of penalty would be inappropriately low if it was limited to £600 a day. An authorised officer must take account of all relevant considerations when making the decision that the penalty would be inappropriately low if it were not increased to up to £1 million. (Read section 21A.6).

21A.4.4 Penalties for failing to comply with information notices given under section 310A or section 311C

A promotor or scheme user who fails to comply with an information notice from HMRC under section 310A of the Finance Act 2004 (section 21.7 has more information) is liable to a penalty.

A promoter or person involved in the supply of a scheme failing to comply with an information notice from HMRC under s311C Finance Act 2004 is liable to a penalty.

With one exception, the person is liable to a penalty of up to a maximum of £600 per day in a set period.

The set period starts on the day after the date by which the person was required to comply with the information notice. (read section 21A.4.5).

The set period ends on the earlier of the day before:

the day on which the person complies with the information notice later than the due date and

the day on which the authorised officer determines the penalty

The maximum penalty may be increased up to £1 million if the authorised officer considers that the amount of penalty would be inappropriately low if it was limited to £600 a day. An authorised officer must take account of all relevant considerations when making the decision that the penalty would be inappropriately low if it were not increased to up to £1 million. (Read section 21A.6).

21A.4.5 Dates by which a person is required to comply with their DOTAS obligations

For guidance on these dates, read:

section 10.2.1 in relation to disclosure of a scheme under section 308 by a promoter

section 10.4 in relation to disclosure of a scheme under section 309 by a user of a scheme with no UK promoter

section 10.6 in relation to disclosure of a scheme under section 310 by a user of a scheme with no promoter

section 20.7 in relation to a request made by HMRC for further information and documents under section 310A

section 20.9 in relation for a request made by HMRC to provide further information and documents under section 311C

21A.4.6 Further Penalties

If a person continues to fail to comply with one of the duties listed after a first or even subsequent penalty has been determined, HMRC may determine further penalties of up to £600 a day:

commencing on the day after the previous penalty period for the same failure ended

ending on the day before the further penalty is determined

21A.5 Cases where either a section 306A or 314A order has been made

A section 306A order issued by a tribunal determines that a scheme is to be treated as notifiable.

A section 314A order issued by a tribunal determines that a scheme is notifiable. It has the effect of confirming that the scheme is, and was always, notifiable within the normal time limits prescribed in the Information Regulations (SI 2012/1836). Section 10.2.1 has more information.

Arrangements must be disclosed to HMRC within 10 business days, beginning with the day after a s306A or s314A order is made (sections 20.5 and 20.6).

The law provides that the promoter cannot rely on doubt as to notifiability as a reasonable excuse for not providing the prescribed information about the scheme within 10 business days of the tribunal making the order.

This does not mean that penalties will definitely be determined against on the promoter if it does not provide the prescribed information within 10 days of the order.

However, any contention the promoter makes that it should not be made liable for penalties because it has a reasonable excuse cannot depend on there being doubt about whether or not the scheme is notifiable.

If the promoter does not disclose the scheme within 10 business days of the order being made, the amount of the penalty, for the first or further penalties in relation to the failure increases to up to £5,000 for each day that the failure continues after the 10 days.

Weekends, bank holidays, Good Friday and Christmas Day are not counted in calculating the 10 business days.

In cases where a 314A order is made, the higher daily penalty is in addition to any penalties at up to £600 for the period ending 11 days after the date on which the order was issued.

If a tribunal subsequently issues an order under section 314A following a s306A order or the person agrees that the scheme was disclosable and that they were required to have disclosed it before the section 306A order was made, HMRC may determine a further penalty. This penalty will relate to the period starting on the date by which the scheme should have been disclosed and ending 10 business days after the section 306A order or, if earlier, on the day before the prescribed information was provided. Any backdated penalty would be at the lower maximum rate of £600 per day.

Where a tribunal has made an order under section 310A requiring more information about a scheme in respect of which a tribunal has given an order under section 306A or section 314A the maximum penalty for failing to comply with the section 310A order is £5,000 a day.

If the maximum penalty that can be determined using the daily penalty described is less than £1 million for the first penalty determined a higher penalty of up to £1 million may be imposed, after taking account all relevant considerations.

21A.6 Determining the Amount of the Penalty: sections 308(1) and (3), 309, 310, 310A and 311C Finance Act 2004 duty failures

The authorised officer will consider all relevant information and evidence available to them, including any representations, when deciding what amount of penalty to charge.

When making their decision about the amount of penalty to charge a promoter or supplier, the authorised officer must have regard to section 315 (B)(2), Finance Act 2004:

setting the penalty at an amount that appears appropriate for deterring the person liable to the penalty and others from similar failures to comply on future occasions

the amount of fees that the person who is being charged the penalty has or is likely to have received in connection with the proposal or arrangements concerned

When making their decision about the amount of penalty to impose on a person who has used a DOTAS scheme in order to obtain a tax advantage for themselves, the authorised officer must have regard to:

setting the penalty at an amount that appears appropriate for deterring the person liable to the penalty and others from similar failures to comply on future occasions

the amount of fees that the person who is being charged the penalty has or is likely to have received in connection with the proposal or arrangements concerned

the amount of any tax advantage that the user of the arrangements gained or sought to gain by participating in the scheme

Consideration of the fees that a person has or has likely received will include amounts that are not necessarily called or invoiced as a fee but are the economic equivalent of a fee. Where precise details of the fees received are not known, the authorised officer will consider using a just and reasonable estimate of what is likely to have been received (HMRC v IPS Progression Limited [224] UKFTT 136] and HMRC v Saxonside Limited (in liquidation) [2025] UKFTT 370.

When deciding which factors are relevant to the case before them, the authorised officer will, to start with, consider the factors that Henderson LJ referred to as “the usual considerations which apply when imposing a [tax] penalty” [paragraph 88 in Revenue and Customs Commissioners v Tager [2018] EWCA Civ 1727]:

i.“reasons for non-compliance”

ii.“the extent to which the position has been remedied”

iii.“the gravity and duration of the non-compliance”. The duration of non-compliance will already be taken into account by the fact the maximum penalty that may be imposed increases for each day of the failure. No additional weight or reduction will therefore be given depending on when the failure is remedied.

iv.“the presence of aggravating or mitigating factors”

v.“the availability of other methods for HMRC to recover the tax at risk”. However, we do not expect this to be a relevant consideration when determining a DOTAS penalty for a promoter or supplier’s failure to comply with a DOTAS duty.

Any other factors that the authorised officer may take into account will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case.

In taking account of any factors when determining the amount of penalty the authorised officer will:

consider the facts and evidence before them

decide which of the facts and evidence are relevant in making the decision about the amount of penalty to be imposed

what weight should be given to each relevant factor. This, again, will depend on the facts and circumstances of each case

21A.7 Information Penalties

Information penalties apply to the following instances of failure to provide prescribed information by the due date and in the form and manner specified in this guidance:

a promoter who does not respond to a pre-disclosure enquiry when required to do so (section 20.4.1 and section 20.4.2 have more information)

an introducer who does not provide, when required to do so, the identity of the person who supplied them with information about the scheme or persons with whom the introducer has made marketing contacts (section 20.4.3 has more information)

a promoter or person involved with the supply of a scheme who does not provide their client with a scheme reference number and with the further required information as supplied for this purpose by HMRC (section 16.2 has more information)

a client of a promoter or of a supplier who fails to provide the scheme reference number to any other person whom they might reasonably expect to be a party to the arrangements and expected to obtain a tax advantage from using it (section 16.3)

a promoter or other supplier who fails to provide HMRC with details of a client to whom they are obliged to issue a scheme reference number (section 19 has more information)

a promoter or other supplier that does not supply further information on parties to the arrangement when required to do so by written notice (section 20 has more information)

an employer who fails to provide the scheme reference number to employees in relation to whose employments a tax advantage is expected to arise (section 14.3.1 has more information)

an employer who fails to provide HMRC with information about employees to whom it is required to provide a scheme reference number (section 16.8 has more information)

a client who does not provide to a promoter or supplier their National Insurance number, UTR or assurances that neither applies (section 16.4 has more information)

a person who fails to tell HMRC the scheme reference number notified to them by a promoter or supplier and the time when the person expects to obtain the tax advantage under the arrangements (section 14.5 has more information)

a promoter or supplier who fails to provide updated information about themselves and the scheme (section 14.9.1 has more information)

In each case the failure includes cases where information is provided after the end of the period prescribed in the Information Regulations (SI 2012/1836) or in a format other than that specified in the DOTAS guidance.

For all of the information penalties listed, HMRC may determine a first penalty for each failure of an amount not exceeding £5,000.

If the failure to provide information continues after a penalty has been determined, HMRC may determine a daily penalty up to £600 a day that the failure continues.

The legislation does not specify how to arrive at the amount of penalty for these failures. However, given that the penalty amount is “up to” £5000, account will be given to any relevant aggravating or mitigating circumstances when arriving at the appropriate penalty figure.

Therefore, when determining penalties for these failures the general and applicable principles established in Tager & Ors v HMRC [2018] EWCA Civ 1727 (‘Tager’) at [88] should be followed to reach a fair and proportionate outcome. (Read section 21A.6).

21A.8 The user penalty — tax advantage

A scheme user who fails to comply with a section 313 obligation to report a scheme reference number and related information (on a return or separately, as prescribed in the Information Regulations (SI 2012/1836)) is, from 26 March 2015, liable to a penalty of:

£5,000 per scheme (for example, each scheme to which the failure relates) for a first occasion

£7,500 per scheme on the second occasion within 3 years (whether or not it relates to the same scheme involved in the previous occasion)

£10,000 per scheme on the third and subsequent occasions (whether or not the failure relates to schemes involved in a previous occasion)

Before that date the penalty was £100 for a first occasion, £500 for a second occasion and £1,000 on third and subsequent occasions.

A scheme user, who is required to report this information on a return does not satisfy their obligations under section 313 unless they enter the information in the boxes provided for that purpose on the return.

For instance, including the scheme reference number or numbers in the ‘white space’ box on returns does not meet the user’s obligation to report the scheme reference number.

You may incur penalties up to £10,000 per scheme if you do not report the scheme reference number on your return in the boxes on the return specified for this purpose or in the form and manner specified if a report is to be made separately from a return. These penalties are determined by HMRC.

21A.9 Legal and Professional Privilege

A legal professional is entitled to make representations to HMRC explaining why their details should not be published. A legal professional can also make a declaration that their representations are true but that they are not able to provide further evidence or explanations in support of the representations because doing so would involve them disclosing privileged communications. Read section 22.2.

A person who carelessly or deliberately includes incorrect information in such a declaration is liable to a penalty of up to £10,000 under section 210 Finance Act 2026.

22. Publishing information under DOTAS (s316C of the Finance Act 2004 and s212 Finance Act 2026)

22.1 General S316C FA 2004

HMRC is entitled to publish information about schemes to which an SRN has been allocated and about their promoters. In certain circumstances, HMRC is also entitled to publish information identifying suppliers of such schemes.

Where a promoter is required to disclose a notifiable scheme to HMRC and has done so, and HMRC allocates the scheme an SRN, HMRC is entitled to name any person who is or has been a promoter of that scheme. This includes publicly naming promoters who are resident outside of the UK.

When HMRC allocates an SRN to a scheme without it having previously been disclosed by a promoter, HMRC is entitled to name any person who is or has been a promoter, including if they are not UK resident.

When HMRC allocates an SRN to a scheme without it having previously been disclosed, HMRC is also entitled to name publicly a person who is not a promoter but has otherwise been involved in the supply of that scheme. However, HMRC can name such a person only if they have been actively involved in the supply of the scheme to which it has allocated the SRN after 9 June 2021.

For schemes that have a main benefit of obtaining a contributions advantage but do not have a main benefit of obtaining a tax advantage, HMRC can name such a person only if they have been actively involved in the supply of the scheme to which HMRC has allocated the SRN after 31 May 2022.

22.2 Information that HMRC may publish — Section 316C FA2004

HMRC may publish the following information:

the name and address of the promoter or other persons involved in the supply of the arrangements (if the involvement of the latter did not come to an end before 10 June 2021)

any of the information prescribed for the purposes of making the disclosure

a summary of the scheme and any name or names it is known by

the statutory provisions on which the tax advantage is based

any ruling of a court or tribunal relating to the scheme or promoter

any other information which HMRC considers it appropriate to publish in order to identify the scheme or a promoter or other persons involved in the supply of it

No information identifying any persons who enter into the scheme may be published under s316C of the Finance Act 2004. But where a promoter or person involved in the supply of the arrangements also entered into the scheme, this does not prevent HMRC publishing information about the promoter or supplier in relation to its activities as a promoter or supplier.

HMRC may also publish any ruling by a court or tribunal relating to any such arrangements or any such ruling relating to the promoter in that person’s capacity as a promoter in relation to a notifiable proposal or arrangements.

This provision is limited to court rulings given after 25 March 2015. HMRC may publish the number of persons who have entered into a scheme.

This information will generally be obtained from the promoter or supplier when it is required to provide client lists to HMRC under section 313ZA (section 19.2).

HMRC may publish that a scheme is ‘APN relevant’ if it may exercise its power to issue accelerated payment notices (APNs) to users of the scheme because the scheme meets the definitional criteria for eligible ‘DOTAS arrangements’ set out at s219 of the Finance Act 2014.

HMRC may also publish that a scheme is APN relevant if it has included the SRN allocated to the scheme on the list of schemes whose users HMRC may issue with an accelerated payment notice.

The information may be published in any manner that HMRC considers appropriate. In the first instance, information will be published on GOV.UK.

22.3 Opportunity to make representations s316C FA2004

In any case where HMRC is considering publishing information about a person who is a promoter or otherwise involved in the supply of a scheme, HMRC is required to inform that person that it is considering doing so and to give the person a reasonable opportunity to make representations about whether the information about them as a promoter or other supplier should be published.

HMRC will give the person a reasonable time in which to make any representations, usually 30 days from when HMRC tells them it is considering publishing the information. This may be longer if agreed. HMRC will consider all representations made and, if necessary, seek further details before making a final decision about publishing information. Either way HMRC will keep the person concerned informed of its decision.

HMRC will not publish details of any person where it concludes they are neither a promoter in relation to the relevant scheme nor have they otherwise been involved in the supply of the arrangements or proposed arrangements.

The decision to publish information about a scheme, including details about a promoter or person involved in the supply of the arrangements will be made by a senior manager within HMRC that is outside of the directorate who is considering publishing information.

22.4 Lawyers and Legal Professional Privilege (LPP) S316C FA04

A lawyer, who promotes a scheme, is deemed not to be a promoter under the DOTAS rules if LPP would prevent them from making a fully compliant disclosure of that scheme if it were notifiable section 3.11. HMRC is therefore not entitled to publicly name such a lawyer as a promoter of that scheme.

A lawyer, who promotes a scheme but is treated as not being a promoter for DOTAS, may still be subject to DOTAS as a person involved in the supply of the scheme they promoted or otherwise advised on. Accordingly, a legal professional may be named on the basis they are a supplier of arrangements, but only if HMRC has allocated an SRN to those arrangements in a subsection (3). (Read section 13.4).

A lawyer may therefore be within any of the definitions of a person about whom information may be published, and therefore within the scope of publishing. A lawyer in this context means a person who could either maintain a claim to legal professional privilege in legal proceedings or, in Scotland, maintain a claim to confidentiality of proceedings.

If HMRC notify a lawyer that they intend to publish information identifying the lawyer, and the lawyer intends making representations to the effect that the information should not be published, they may not be able to confirm the accuracy of those representations without disclosing the content of privileged communications.

In these cases, a lawyer can make a declaration under s209 of the Finance Act 2026 alongside representations. This submission to HMRC first requires a lawyer to declare that the representations are true. The submission must also include a declaration that the content of privileged communications would be sufficient (whether alone or with other information) to show HMRC that the representations are true on the balance of probabilities.

A declaration must be provided to HMRC no later than the representations to which it relates.

HMRC, or a court or tribunal in any proceedings, must treat a declaration made by a lawyer in relation to whether information may be published as conclusive evidence of the information contained in the declaration.

However, this will not be the case if HMRC or a court or tribunal are satisfied that the declaration contains incorrect information based, for example on evidence that may have come to light during taxpayer enquiries. A person making a declaration who carelessly or deliberately includes incorrect information may be liable to a penalty.

22.5 Suppliers S316C FA04

Depending on the circumstances of a case and the evidence provided, including by way of representations, HMRC may use its discretion not to publish information about a supplier. Each case will be determined on its own merits.

It will be appropriate for HMRC to take account of the extent of the supplier’s involvement in the design or marketing of the scheme, its role in the implementation or operation of the scheme, the rewards it received for its activities in connection with the scheme.

Other factors that it may be relevant to take into account when making the decision whether to publish such a supplier’s information and which suppliers may wish to cover in their representations include:

the supplier’s tax and professional knowledge

their awareness of the elements of the scheme which were intended to give rise to a tax advantage at the time they were actively involved with the scheme

whether the supplier adhered to professional standards

whether the supplier exercised due diligence and made necessary checks

whether the supplier or tax professional gave HMRC information early enough to identify the promoter

22.6 Information HMRC must publish after a court ruling that is relevant to arrangements about which HMRC has published information S316D FA2004

If HMRC has published information about tax arrangements under section 316C of the Finance Act 2004 and there is a final ruling by a court or tribunal based on principles or reasoning which, if applied to the scheme, would allow the tax advantage claimed to arise from the scheme, HMRC must publish information about the ruling.

HMRC must publish this information in the same manner as it published the information under section 316C.

A ruling is final if it is:

of the Supreme Court

in respect of which no appeal or further appeal may be made

22.7 Publication following an incorrect declaration by a lawyer S212 FA2026

An authorised officer may publish information about a person where the person has incurred a penalty for making an incorrect declaration under s209 Finance Act 2026 and that penalty has become final. Publishing that a person is liable for a penalty following an incorrect declaration must take place within 12 months of the date on which the penalty becomes final.
